This classic text appears here in a new edition for the first time in four decades. The new 
edition, with the aid of two new authors, brings it up to date for a new generation of math-
ematicians and mathematics students.

Elements of Algebraic Topology provides the most concrete approach to the subject. With 
coverage of homology and cohomology theory, universal coefficient theorems, Kunneth 
theorem, duality in manifolds, and applications to classical theorems of point-set topol-
ogy, this book is perfect for communicating complex topics and the fun nature of algebraic 
topology for beginners.

This second edition retains the essential features of the original book. Most of the notation 
and terminology are the same. There are some useful additions. There is a new introduction 
to homotopy theory. A new Index of Notation is included. Many new exercises are added.

Algebraic topology is a cornerstone of modern mathematics. Every working mathemati-
cian should have at least an acquaintance with the subject. This book, which is based 
largely on the theory of triangulations, provides such an introduction. It should be acces-
sible to a broad cross-section of the profession—both students and senior mathemati-
cians. Students should have some familiarity with general topology.

James R. Munkres served on the MIT Mathematics Faculty from 1960-2000 and continues 
as a senior lecturer. He earned a PhD in mathematics from the University of Michigan under 
the supervision of Edwin Moise in 1956. Prof. Munkres is a differential topologist and is 
also responsible for the Munkres Assignment Algorithm. He authored numerous texts. His 
distinctions include the MIT School of Science Teaching Prize for Undergraduate Education 
in 1984, and an Honorary Doctorate from Nebraska Wesleyan University in 1989.

Steven G. Krantz is a professor at Washington University in St. Louis where he teaches 
mathematics. He earned his PhD from Princeton University and since then has taught at 
UCLA, Princeton University, and Pennsylvania State University. Dr. Krantz has written 
over 175 scholarly papers and more than 65 books. He is the founding editor of the Journal 
of Geometric Analysis. He was named a fellow of the American Mathematical Society and 
has received the Chauvenet Prize, Beckenbach Book Award, and Kemper Prize.

Harold R. Parks earned his PhD in mathematics from Princeton University. He was a 
J.D. Tamarkin Instructor at Brown University. He then assumed a tenure-track position 
at Oregon State University. He was promoted to professor in 1989. He spent the academic 
year 1982-1983 at Indiana University as a visiting associate professor. During his time in 
the Mathematics Department of Oregon State, he served at various times as Assistant 
Department Chair, Associate Department Chair, and Department Chair. He has written 
8 books and 42 scholarly papers, edits 2 journals, and is an AMS Fellow.

Algebraic topology is a cornerstone of modern mathematics. Every working
mathematician should have at least an acquaintance with the subject. The
book Elements of Algebraic Topology by James R. Munkres is a classic that
provides such an introduction. It is now forty years old and needs to be brought
up to date. This new edition is meant to fulfill that purpose.

Of course, we have retained the essential features of the original book.
Most of the notation is the same and most of the terminology is the same. We
have retained all of the key topics from the first edition. But there are some
useful additions and changes.

Unlike the first edition, we do give an introduction to homotopy theory
in a section on the fundamental group. The section on acyclic models has
been completely revamped to make it more accessible to the reader. We have
collected together at the end some very limited biographical information about
each person mentioned in the text. There is also a short list of additional
readings, mostly chosen from books published after the first edition. Another
new feature is a very detailed Index of Notation. And the main Index for
the book is now also very detailed. Finally, we have added quite a number of
exercises. Most of these are in the nature of drill.
Organization of this book

The first two chapters are based on simplicial homology—the most concrete of
homology theories—so they should be quite accessible to students. The third
chapter introduces material that is more abstract, including the Eilenberg–
Steenrod Axioms. The fourth chapter introduces the singular homology theory
and many interesting applications. CW complexes appear as a computational
tool. For a one-semester course, these first four chapters would be suitable.

Sections marked with asterisks may be considered optional for this one-
semester course. Of course, the applications seem to the authors to be of great
interest, so while optional, the choice may well be to cover some or all of them.

Cohomology theory is introduced in the fifth chapter, culminating with
the cohomology ring. The sixth chapter introduces the tensor product and
adds to the treatment of homology with arbitrary coefficients mentioned
in an optional section in the first chapter. While likely too much for a

one-semester course, the first six chapters do provide a solid core that should
be accessible to a broad cross-section of the profession—both students and
senior mathematicians.

For a two-semester course, the entire book may be appropriate. Of course,
the instructor will have to exercise some discretion in designing a suitable
course. Sections that are optional for the one-semester course (for example,
Categories and Functors) may be necessary for the two-semester course. The
last two chapters are independent of each other. So if it is necessary to cut
some material as the second semester winds down, it can be done.

Regarding the last two chapters, the seventh chapter deals with homologi-
cal algebra, including the universal coefficient theorems and the K¨unneth theo-
rems in various settings. The eighth chapter deals with manifolds—specifically,
the duality theorems associated with the names of Poincar´e, Lefschetz, Alexan-
der, and Pontryagin. ˇCech cohomology is introduced to study Pontryagin du-
ality.

If an instructor wishes to spend less time on the treatment of simplicial
homology, then it is possible to omit Chapter 2. In that case, the topological
invariance of the simplicial homology groups will not be shown directly, but
instead must be obtained via the invariance of the singular homology groups
and the isomorphism between simplicial and singular homology.

We take it that the student has some familiarity with general topology. This
includes compactness, connectedness, and quotient spaces. The Tietze exten-
sion theorem for normal spaces will be used, and quotient spaces are very
important. Quotient spaces are reviewed at appropriate times.

We also would like the student to know some algebra. Notably some fa-
miliarity with groups, factor groups, and homomorphisms as well as rings,
fields, and vector spaces. No particularly deep theorems will be needed. As
with quotient spaces, basic algebra results are reviewed at appropriate times.

For our cover figure, we are grateful to Carlo H. S´equin of the University
of California at Berkeley. The figure shows how two M¨obius bands can fit
together to form a Klein bottle.

We are grateful to our Editor Robert Ross for his support and encourage-
ment. We look forward to feedback from our readership.
Homology Groups of a Simplicial Complex

A fundamental problem of topology is that of determining, for two spaces,
whether or not they are homeomorphic. To show two spaces are homeomor-
phic, one needs to construct a continuous bijective map, with a continuous
inverse, mapping one space to the other. To show two spaces are not homeo-
morphic involves showing that such a map does not exist. To do that is often
harder. The usual way of proceeding is to find some topological property [i.e.,
some property invariant under homeomorphisms] that is satisfied by one space
but not the other. For example, the closed unit disc in R2 cannot be homeo-
morphic with the plane R2, because the closed disc is compact and the plane
is not. Nor can the real line R be homeomorphic with R2, because deleting
a point from R leaves a disconnected space remaining, while deleting a point
from R2 does not.

Such elementary properties do not carry one very far in tackling homeo-
morphism problems. Classifying all compact surfaces up to homeomorphism,
for instance, demands more sophisticated topological invariants than these.
So does the problem of showing that, in general, Rn and Rm are not homeo-
morphic if n̸ = m.

Algebraic topology originated in the attempts by such mathematicians
as Henri Poincar´e and Enrico Betti to construct such topological invariants.
Poincar´e introduced a certain group, called the fundamental group of a topo-
logical space; it is, by its definition, a topological invariant. One can show fairly
readily that a number of familiar spaces, such as the sphere, torus, and Klein
bottle, have fundamental groups that are different, so these spaces cannot be
homeomorphic [see [Mun00], Section 60]. In fact, one can classify all compact
surfaces using the fundamental group [see [Mas91], Chapter 4, Section 5].

The transition from focusing on the numerical invariants of a space to
studying the homology groups of a space was hastened by the algebraist
Emmy Noether. This happened because in the mid-1920s Paul Alexandroff
and Heinz Hopf were visitors at G¨ottingen where Noether was a member of
the department. She recognized that the betti numbers and torsion coefficients
that Alexandroff and Hopf were discussing were in fact invariants associated
with abelian groups: specifically the homology groups. Indeed, Hopf explic-
itly credited the influence of Noether in the introductory section of his 1928

paper [Hop28] in which he generalized the Euler–Poincar´e formula. Early on
the homology groups presented the difficulty that they were not obviously a
topological invariant. Once that was shown, then those groups could also be
used to tackle homeomorphism problems.

We shall begin our discussion of algebraic topology by studying the ho-
mology groups. Later on, we shall deal with other topological invariants, such
as the cohomology groups and the cohomology ring. We shall also give a brief
treatment of the homotopy groups.

There are several different ways of defining homology groups, all of which
lead to the same results for spaces that are sufficiently nice. The two that
we shall consider in detail are the simplicial and the singular groups. We
begin with the simplicial homology groups, which came first historically. Both
conceptually and computationally, they are concrete and down-to-earth. They
are defined, however, only for particularly nice spaces [i.e., polyhedra], and it is
hard work to prove their topological invariance. After that, we shall treat the
singular homology groups, which were introduced as a generalization of the
simplicial groups. They are defined for arbitrary spaces, and it is immediate
from their definition that they are topological invariants. Furthermore, they
are much more convenient for theoretical purposes than the simplicial groups.
They are not as readily computable as the simplicial groups, but they agree
with the simplicial homology groups when both are defined.

A third way of defining homology groups for arbitrary spaces is due to
Eduard ˇCech. The ˇCech homology theory is still not completely satisfactory,
but ˇCech cohomology theory is both important and useful. It will appear near
the end of this book.

Before defining simplicial homology groups, we must discuss the class of spaces
for which they are defined, which is the class of all polyhedra. A polyhedron is
a space that can be built from such building blocks as line segments, triangles,
tetrahedra, and their higher-dimensional analogues, by gluing them together
along their faces. In this section, we shall discuss these basic building blocks,
and in the next, we shall use them to construct polyhedra.

Definition 1.3.1 A simplicial complex K in RN is a collection of simplices
in RN such that
(1) Every face of a simplex of K is in K.
(2) The intersection of any two simplices of K is a face of each of

and its faces, is a simplicial complex. The collection K2, consisting of two

The following lemma is sometimes useful in verifying that a collection of
simplices is a simplicial complex:

Lemma 1.3.3 A collection K of simplices is a simplicial complex if and only
if the following hold:
(1) Every face of a simplex of K is in K.
(2′) Every pair of distinct simplices of K have disjoint interiors.

Homology Groups of a Simplicial Complex

Proof: First, assume K is a simplicial complex. Given two simplices σ and τ
of K we show that if there exists x ∈Int σ ∩Int τ, then σ = τ. Let s = σ ∩τ.
If s were a proper face of σ, then x would belong to Bd σ, which it does not.
Therefore, s = σ. Similarly, s is not a proper face of τ, so s = τ. We conclude
that σ = s = τ.

To prove the converse, we assume (1) and (2′) hold. Let two simplices σ
and τ of K be given. Suppose that σ ∩τ is non-empty. We will show that
σ ∩τ is a face σ′ of σ. Specifically, σ′ is the face of σ spanned by the vertices
b0, b1, . . . , bm of σ that lie in τ. First, σ′ is contained in σ ∩τ because σ ∩τ
is convex and contains b0, b1, . . . , bm. To prove the reverse inclusion, suppose
that x ∈σ ∩τ. Then x ∈Int s ∩Int t, for some face s of σ and some face t of
τ. It follows from (2′) that s = t. Hence the vertices of s lie in τ so that by
definition they are elements of the set {b0, b1, . . . , bm}. Then s is a face of σ′,
as desired. Similarly, we can show that σ ∩τ is a face τ ′ of τ. Thus we have
shown that (2) holds.

It follows from that last lemma that if σ is a simplex, then the collection
consisting of σ and its proper faces is a simplicial complex: Condition (1) is
immediate, and condition (2′) holds because for each point x ∈σ, there is
exactly one face s of σ such that x ∈Int s.

Definition 1.3.4 If L is a subcollection of K that contains all faces of its
elements, then L is a simplicial complex in its own right, called a subcomplex
of K. One subcomplex of K is the collection of all simplices of K of dimension
at most p; it is called the p-skeleton of K and is denoted K(p). The points of
the collection K(0) are called the vertices of K.

Definition 1.3.5 Let |K| be the subset of RN that is the union of the sim-
plices of K. Giving each simplex its natural topology as a subspace of RN, we
then topologize |K| by declaring a subset A of |K| to be closed in |K| if and
only if A ∩σ is closed in σ, for each σ in K. It is easy to see that this defines
a topology on |K|, for this collection of sets is closed under finite unions and
arbitrary intersections. The space |K| is called the underlying space of K, or
the polytope of K.

Elements of Algebraic Topology

A space that is the polytope of a simplicial complex will be called a poly-
hedron. [We note that some topologists reserve this term for the polytope of
a finite simplicial complex.]

In general, the topology of |K| is finer [i.e., larger] than the topology |K|
inherits as a subspace of RN. To see this, note that if A is closed in |K| in
the subspace topology, then A = B ∩|K| for some closed set B in RN. Then
B ∩σ is closed in σ for each simplex σ of K, so A ∩σ = B ∩|K| ∩σ = B ∩σ
is closed in σ. By definition A is closed in the topology of |K|.

The two topologies on |K|, the subspace topology and the topology of Def-
inition 1.3.5, are different in general. [See Examples 1.3.6 and 1.3.7.] Nonethe-
less, if K is finite, the two topologies are the same. For suppose K is finite
and A is closed in |K|. Then A ∩σ is closed in σ and hence closed in RN.
Because A is the union of the finitely many closed sets A ∩σ, the set A also
is closed in RN.

[m, m + 1], where m̸ = 0 is an integer, along with all simplices of the form
[1/(n+1), 1/n] for n a positive integer, along with all faces of these simplices.
Then K is a complex whose underlying space equals R as a set but not as a
topological space. For instance, the set of points of the form 1/n, n > 0, is
closed in |K| but not in R.

EXAMPLE 1.3.7 Let K be the collection of 1-simplices σ1, σ2, . . . and their
vertices, where σi is the 1-simplex in R2 having vertices 0 and (1, 1/i). See
Figure 1.3.2. Then K is a simplicial complex. The intersection of |K| with the

We prove some elementary topological properties of polyhedra.

Lemma 1.3.8 If L is a subcomplex of K, then |L| is a closed subspace of |K|.
In particular, if σ ∈K, then σ is a closed subspace of |K|.

Proof: Suppose A is closed in |L|. If σ is a simplex of K, then σ ∩|L| is the
union of those faces si of σ that belong to L. Since A is closed in |L|, the set
A ∩si is closed in si and hence closed in σ. Since A ∩σ is a finite union of the
sets A ∩si, it is closed in σ. We conclude that A is closed in |K|.

Conversely, if B is closed in |K|, then B ∩σ is closed in σ for each σ ∈K,
and in particular for each σ ∈L. Hence B ∩|L| is closed in |L|.

Lemma 1.3.9 A map f : |K| →X is continuous if and only if f|σ is con-
tinuous for each σ ∈K.

Proof: If f is continuous, so is f|σ since σ is a subspace of |K|. Conversely,
suppose each map f|σ is continuous. If C is a closed set of X, then f −1(C∩σ) =
(f|σ)−1(C), which is closed in σ by the continuity of f|σ. Thus f −1(C) is
closed in |K| by definition.

Definition 1.3.10 If X is a space and if C is a collection of subspaces of X
whose union is X, then the topology of X is said to be coherent with the
collection C, provided a set A is closed in X if and only if A ∩C is closed in
C for each C ∈C. It is equivalent to require that U be open in X if and only
if U ∩C is open in C for each C ∈C.

In particular, the topology of |K| is coherent with the collection of sub-
spaces σ, for σ ∈K.

The analogue of Lemma 1.3.9 holds for coherent topologies in general: a
map f : X →Y is continuous if and only if f|C is continuous for each C ∈C.

Lemma 1.3.13 If K is finite, then |K| is compact. Conversely, if a subset A
of |K| is compact, then A ⊂|K0| for some finite subcomplex K0 of K.

Proof: If K is finite, then |K| is a finite union of compact subspaces σ, and
hence is compact.

Now suppose that A ⊂|K| is compact and A does not lie in the polytope of
any finite subcomplex of K. Choose a point xs ∈A ∩Int s whenever A ∩Int s

B is closed, since its intersection with any simplex σ is finite. Being closed and
discrete, B has no limit point, contrary to the fact that every infinite subset
of a compact space has a limit point.

Three particular subspaces of |K| are often useful when studying local
properties of |K|. We mention them here.

Definition 1.3.14 If v is a vertex of K, the star of v in K, denoted by St v,
or sometimes by St(v, K), is the union of the interiors of those simplices of K
that have v as a vertex. Its closure, denoted St v, is called the closed star of
v in K. It is the union of all simplices of K having v as a vertex, and is the
polytope of a subcomplex of K. The set St v \ St v is called the link of v in
K and is denoted Lk v. See Figure 1.3.3.

The set St v is open in |K|, since it consists of all points x of |K| such
that tv(x) > 0. Its complement is the union of all simplices of K that do not

Definition 1.3.15 A simplicial complex K is said to be locally finite if each
vertex of K belongs to only finitely many simplices of K. Said differently, a
complex is locally finite if and only if each closed star St v is the polytope of

is locally compact.

Proof: Suppose K is locally finite. Given x ∈|K|, it lies in St v for some
vertex v of K. Since St v is a compact set, |K| is locally compact. We leave
the converse as an exercise.

General Simplicial Complexes

Our insistence that a simplicial complex K must lie in RN for some N puts
a limitation on the cardinality of K and on the dimension of the simplices of
K. We now remove these restrictions.

Homology Groups of a Simplicial Complex
15

Let J be an arbitrary index set, and let RJ denote the J-fold cartesian
product of R with itself. An element of RJ is a function from J to R, ordinarily
denoted using the “tuple notation” (xα)α∈J. The product RJ is of course a
vector space with the usual component-wise addition and multiplication by
scalars.

Let EJ denote the subset of RJ consisting of all points (xα)α∈J such that
xα = 0 for all but finitely many values of α. Note that EJ is a vector subspace
of (xα)α∈J. If ϵα ∈EJ is the map of J into R whose value is 1 on the index α
and is 0 on all other elements of J, then the set {ϵα : α ∈J} is a basis for EJ
[but not for RJ, if J is infinite].
We call EJ generalized euclidean space and topologize it by the metric

Everything we have done for complexes in RN generalizes to complexes in
EJ. The space EJ is the union of certain of its finite-dimensional subspaces—
namely, the subspaces spanned by finite subsets of the basis {ϵα : α ∈J}.
Each such subspace is simply a copy of RN for some N. Any finite set
{a0, a1, . . . , an} of points of EJ lies in such a subspace. If the points are geo-
metrically independent, then the simplex they span lies in the same subspace.
Furthermore, the metric on EJ gives the usual topology on each such sub-
space. Therefore, any finite collection of simplices in EJ lies in a copy of RN

for some N. All that we are really doing is to allow ourselves to deal with
complexes for which the total collection of simplices cannot be fitted entirely
into any one RN. Conceptually it may seem more complicated to work in EJ
than in RN, but in practice, it causes no difficulty at all.

We leave it to you to check that our results hold for complexes in EJ. We
shall use these results freely henceforth.

Let us make one further comment. If K is a complex in RN, then each
simplex of K has dimension at most N. On the other hand, if K is a complex
in EJ, there need be no upper bound on the dimensions of the simplices of K.
We define the dimension of K, denoted dim K, to be the largest dimension
of a simplex of K, if such a maximum exists; otherwise, we say that K has
infinite dimension.

1.4
Abstract Simplicial Complexes

In practice, specifying a polyhedron X by giving a collection of simplices whose
union is X is not a very convenient way of dealing with specific polyhedra. One
quickly gets immersed in details of analytic geometry; it is messy to specify
all the simplices and to make sure they intersect only when they should. It
is much easier to specify X by means of an “abstract simplicial complex,” a
notion we now introduce.

Definition 1.4.1 An abstract simplicial complex is a collection S of finite
nonempty sets, such that if A is an element of S, then so is every nonempty
subset of A.

The element A of S is called a simplex of S; its dimension is one less than
the number of its elements. Each nonempty subset of A is called a face of A.

Homology Groups of a Simplicial Complex
17

The dimension of S is the largest dimension of one of its simplices or is infinite
if there is no such largest dimension. The vertex set V of S is the union of
the one-point elements of S; we shall make no distinction between the vertex
v ∈V and the 0-simplex {v} ∈S. A subcollection of S that is itself a complex
is called a subcomplex of S.

Two abstract complexes S and T are said to be isomorphic if there is a
bijective correspondence f mapping the vertex set of S to the vertex set of T
such that {a0, a1, . . . , an} ∈S if and only if {f(a0), f(a1), . . . , f(an)} ∈T .

Definition 1.4.2 If K is a simplicial complex, let V be the vertex set of
K. Let K be the collection of all subsets {a0, a1, . . . , an} of V such that the
vertices a0, a1, . . . , an span a simplex of K. The collection K is called the
vertex scheme of K.

The collection K is a particular example of an abstract simplicial complex.
It is in fact the crucial example, as the following theorem shows.

1.7
Homology Groups of Surfaces

If K is a finite complex, then the chain group Cp(K) has finite rank, so the
cycle group Zp(K) also has finite rank. Then Hp(K) is finitely generated, so
that the fundamental theorem of abelian groups applies. The betti number
and torsion coefficients of Hp(K) are called, classically, the betti number of K
and the torsion coefficients of K in dimension p. The fact that these numbers
are topological invariants of |K| will be proved in Chapter 2.

In former times, much attention was paid to the numerical invariants,
not only in topology, but also in algebra and other parts of mathematics.
Nowadays, mathematicians are likely to feel that homology groups are the
more important notion, and one is more likely to study properties of these
groups than to compute their numerical invariants. Nevertheless, it is still
important in many situations to compute the homology groups specifically—
that is, to find the betti numbers and torsion coefficients for a given space.

One of the greatest virtues of the simplicial homology groups is that it is
in fact possible to do precisely this. In Section 1.12 we shall prove a theorem
to the effect that, for a finite complex K, the homology groups are effectively
computable. This means that there is a specific algorithm for finding the betti
numbers and torsion coefficients of K.

In the present section, we shall compute the betti numbers and torsion
coefficients of the compact surfaces. The techniques we shall use may seem a
bit awkward and ad hoc in nature. But, in fact, they are effective on a large
class of spaces. In a later section, when we study CW complexes, we shall
return to these techniques and show they are part of a systematic approach
to computing homology groups.

being open in P, would contain an interval of points on this line segment. But
the ray from w through x intersects |K| in only one point, by hypothesis.

Suppose that K0 is a subcomplex of the complex K. In many of the appli-

If K0 is a subcomplex of the complex K, then the chain group Cp(K0) can

1.12
∗The Computability of Homology Groups

We have computed the homology groups of some familiar spaces, such as the
sphere and the torus and the Klein bottle. Now we ask the question whether
one can in fact compute homology groups in general. For finite complexes,
the answer is affirmative. In this section, we present an explicit algorithm for
carrying out the computation.

standard bases for free chain complexes. A third corollary gives our desired
algorithm for computing the homology groups of a finite complex.

Topological Invariance of the Homology
Groups

In Chapter 1, we defined a function which assigns to each simplicial complex
K a sequence of abelian groups called the homology groups of K. Our purpose
now is to show that these groups are determined by the topology of K.

We shall attack this problem by studying continuous maps from one
polyhedron to another; we are particularly interested in what such a map
does to the homology groups. We will in fact prove that a continuous map
h : |K| →|L| of polyhedra induces, in a canonical fashion, a homomorphism
h∗: Hp(K) →Hp(L) of the homology groups of the corresponding simplicial
complexes. Constructing this homomorphism will entail a fair bit of work.

We will see that when h is a homeomorphism of topological spaces, then
h∗is an isomorphism of groups. The topological invariance of the simplicial
homology groups is an immediate consequence.

We can see intuitively why there should be an induced homomorphism of
homology groups. If we think of a homology class as a geometric object, then
it is plausible that its image under h should be a well-defined homology class.
For instance, if X is a topological space, then a closed loop on the surface
T is mapped by h : T →X into a closed loop in X. To make this intuition
rigorous will be our task for some time.

We know that a simplicial map f : |K| →|L| induces a homomorphism of
homology groups. The current chapter is dedicated to the task of showing that
an arbitrary continuous map h can be suitably approximated by a simplicial
map f, and that the resulting induced homomorphism depends only on the
map h, and not on the particular approximation chosen.

2.3
Barycentric Subdivision

We show here that a finite complex may be “subdivided” into simplices that
are as small as we wish. We will use this result in our consideration of simplicial
homology, and later on in our discussion of singular homology in Chapter 4.

Definition 2.3.1 Let K be a geometric complex in EJ. A complex K′ is said
to be a subdivision of K if
(1) Each simplex of K′ is contained in a simplex of K.
(2) Each simplex of K is the union of finitely many simplices of K′.

These conditions imply that the union of the simplices of K′ equals the
union of the simplices of K. That is, |K′| and |K| are equal as sets. The
finiteness part of condition (2) guarantees that |K′| and |K| are equal as
topological spaces. This is easy to check.

Note that if K′′ is a subdivision of K′ and if K′ is a subdivision of K, then
K′′ is a subdivision of K.

Observe that if K′ is a subdivision of K, and if K0 is a subcomplex of K,
then the collection of all simplices of K′ that lie in |K0| is automatically a
subdivision of K0. We in fact call it the subdivision of K0 induced by K′.
The following result will be useful in the sequel.
Lemma 2.3.2 Let K′ be a subdivision of K. Then for each vertex w of K′
there is a vertex v of K such that

St(w, K′) ⊂St(v, K) .
(∗)

In fact, if σ is the simplex of K such that w ∈Int σ, then this inclusion holds
precisely when v is a vertex of σ.

Proof: If the inclusion (∗) holds, then since w belongs to St(w, K′), so w must
lie in some open simplex of K that has v as a vertex.

Conversely, suppose that w ∈Int σ and v is a vertex of σ. It suffices to
show that
|K| \ St(v, K) ⊂|K| \ St(w, K′) .

The set on the left-hand side of this last inclusion is the union of all simplices of
K that do not have v as a vertex. Hence it is also a union of simplices τ of K′.
No such simplex τ can have w as a vertex, just because w ∈Int σ ⊂St(v, K).
Thus any such simplex lies in |K| \ St(w, K′).

2.4
The Simplicial Approximation Theorem

We now show that if h : |K| →|L| is a continuous map, then there is a
subdivision K′ of K such that h has a simplicial approximation f : K′ →L.
The proof when K is finite follows easily from the results of the preceding
section; barycentric subdivision will suffice. The general case requires a slightly
more sophisticated technique of subdivision, called “generalized barycentric
subdivision,” that we will describe below in Definition 2.4.5.
We will have need of the following lemma:

Lemma 2.4.1 (Lebesgue’s covering lemma) For every open cover, A, of
a compact metric space, there exists a positive real number λ such that every
subset of diameter less than λ is contained in some element of A.
The positive number λ is called a Lebesgue number for A.

Proof: If there were no such λ, then one could choose a sequence Cn of sets,
where Cn has diameter less than 1/n but does not lie in any element of A.
Choose xn ∈Cn; by compactness, some subsequence xni converges to some
element x. Now x ∈A for some A ∈A. Because A is open, it contains Cni for
i sufficiently large, contrary to our construction.

Theorem 2.4.2 (The finite simplicial approximation theorem) Let K
and L be complexes, and assume that K is finite. Given a continuous map
h : |K| →|L|, there is an N such that h has a simplicial approximation
f : sdNK →L.

Proof: Cover |K| by the open sets h−1(St w) as w ranges over the vertices of
L. Now given this open covering A of the compact metric space |K|, we let λ
be a Lebesgue number for A.

Choose N so that each simplex in sdNK has diameter less than λ/2. Then
each star of a vertex in sdNk has diameter less than λ, so it lies in one of
the sets h−1(St w). Then h : |K| →|L| satisfies the star condition relative to
sdNK and L, and the desired simplicial approximation exists.

We know that if two spaces are homeomorphic then they have isomorphic

Definition 2.7.8 Two spaces X and Y are said to be homotopy equivalent,

Symmetry and reflexivity of this relation are trivial. Transitivity is left as

constant.

2.8
Review of Quotient Spaces
In this section we review some of the basic ideas concerning quotient spaces.

A surjective map p : X →Y is called a quotient map provided that a
subset U ⊂Y is open if and only if p−1(U) ⊂X is open. This condition is
equivalent to requiring that E ⊂Y be closed if and only if p−1(E) ⊂X is
closed.

A subset C of X is saturated with respect to p if it equals the complete
inverse image set p−1(A) for some subset A ⊂Y . To say that p is a quotient
map is to say that p is continuous and p maps saturated open subsets of X
to open subsets of Y (or, equivalently, saturated closed subsets of X to closed
subsets of Y ).

Let p : X →Y be a surjective, continuous map. If p is either an open
map or a closed map (that is, p either maps open sets to open sets or closed
sets to closed sets), then p is a quotient map. In particular, if X is compact
and Y is Hausdorff, then p is a closed map and hence a quotient map.

First we list some elementary facts about quotient maps. Their proofs are
straightforward and we leave them to the reader.
• A one-to-one quotient map is a homeomorphism.
• The composition of quotient maps is a quotient map.

• The restriction of a quotient map can sometimes be a quotient map. If
p : X →Y is a quotient map, and if A ⊂X is a saturated subspace that is
either open or closed, then p restricted to A is a quotient map.

Continuous maps and quotient maps are related as follows: If p : X →Y
is a quotient map and f : X →Z is a continuous map that is constant on
each set p−1(y), then there is a unique continuous map g : Y →Z such that
g ◦p = f. We say that g is induced by f. See the diagram.

Relative Homology and the
Eilenberg–Steenrod Axioms

Until now we have concentrated primarily on studying the “absolute” simpli-
cial homology groups, though we have defined the relative groups and have
proved their topological invariance. Now we shall study the relative groups
in more detail. These groups have many uses. For one thing, they arise nat-
urally in many of the applications of topology. A second point is that they
are involved in an essential way in expressing those fundamental properties of
homology that are called the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms.

One of the ways that relative homology groups can be useful is for giv-
ing information about the absolute homology groups. There are relationships
between the relative groups Hp(K, K0) and the absolute groups Hp(K) and
Hp(K0). For example, the vanishing of Hp(K, K0) and Hp+1(K, K0) implies
that Hp(K) and Hp(K0) are isomorphic. This fact is not obvious. Formulating
this relationship in a precise and general manner is a subtle problem.

In the early days of algebraic topology, the theorems described above were
often awkward and wordy. There was a need for the right language to express
the ideas. A remarkable algebraic idea due to Eilenberg clarified the matter
notably. Really just a new and convenient notation, it is called an “exact
sequence” (of groups, or rings, or some other algebraic structure). The useful-
ness of this concept, in algebra as well as topology, is difficult to overestimate.
Obscure algebraic arguments often become quite transparent once they are
formulated in terms of exact sequences. Other arguments that were difficult
even for professional algebraists become so straightforward that they can be
safely left to the reader.

If some terminology in this chapter regarding groups seems unfamiliar, the
reader should refer to Section 1.5 for clarification.

3.5
The Eilenberg–Steenrod Axioms

We have defined homology groups for a particular class of spaces—namely,
the polyhedra. Historically these were the first homology groups to be defined.

170
Elements of Algebraic Topology

Later various generalized definitions of homology were formulated that applied
to more general spaces. These various homology theories had many features
in common, and they all gave the same results as simplicial homology theory
on the class of polyhedra.

This plethora of homology theories led Eilenberg and Steenrod to ax-
iomatize the notion of a homology theory. They formulated certain crucial
properties these theories have in common, and showed that these properties
characterize the homology groups completely on the class of polyhedra.

We shall not try to reproduce the axiomatic approach at this point, nor
shall we prove that the axioms characterize homology for polyhedra. For this,
the reader is referred to Eilenberg and Steenrod’s book [ES52]. We shall simply
list the seven axioms here, together with an additional axiom that is needed
when one deals with non-compact spaces. In the next section, we verify that
simplicial homology theory satisfies the axioms.

This situation illustrates a phenomenon that occurs over and over again
in mathematics: A theory formulated for one purpose turns out to have con-
sequences far removed from what its originators envisaged.

3.6
The Axioms for Simplicial Theory

Before showing that simplicial homology theory satisfies the Eilenberg–
Steenrod axioms, we must treat several points of the theory with more care
than we have shown so far. The axioms involve homology groups that are de-
fined on an admissible class of spaces. Strictly speaking, we have not defined
homology groups for spaces, but only for simplicial complexes. Given a polyhe-
dron X, there are many different simplicial complexes whose polytopes equal
X. Their homology groups are isomorphic to one another in a natural way, but
they are nevertheless distinct groups. Similarly, if h : X →Y is a continuous
map where X = |K| and Y = |L|, we have defined an induced homomorphism
h∗: Hp(K) →Hp(L). Of course if X = |M| and Y = |N|, then we also have
an induced homomorphism Hp(M) →Hp(N), which we also denote by h∗.
We have noted this notational ambiguity in an earlier discussion.

The way out of this difficulty is to introduce a new level of abstraction:
Given a polyhedron X, we can consider the class of all simplicial complexes
whose polytopes equal X, and we can identify their homology groups in a
natural way. The resulting groups can be called the homology groups of the
polyhedron X.

More generally, we can perform this same construction for any space that
is homeomorphic to a polyhedron. We give the details in what follows.

Singular Homology Theory

Now we are in some sense going to begin all over again. We construct a new
homology theory. As compared with simplicial theory, it is much more “natu-
ral.” For one thing, the homology groups are defined for arbitrary topological
spaces, not only for triangulable ones. For another, the homomorphism in-
duced by a continuous map is defined directly and its functorial properties
are proved easily; no difficult results such as the simplicial approximation the-
orem are needed. The topological invariance of the singular homology groups
follows at once.

Unfortunately, the singular homology groups are not immediately com-
putable. One must develop a good deal of singular theory before one can
compute the homology of even such a simple space as the sphere Sn. Eventu-
ally, when we develop the theory of CW complexes, we will see how singular
homology can be computed fairly readily. Alternatively, since we shall show
that simplicial and singular homology groups are isomorphic for triangulable
spaces, we can always go back to simplicial theory if we want to compute
something.

In this chapter, we construct the singular homology groups and prove that
they satisfy the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms on the class of all topological
spaces. [The homotopy axiom and the excision axiom, it turns out, require
more effort than the others.] Then we construct a specific isomorphism be-
tween the singular and simplicial theories that will be useful later.

Finally, we give a number of applications. They include the Jordan curve
theorem, theorems about manifolds, and the computation of the homology of
real and complex projective spaces.

4.4
Excision in Singular Homology

In this section we verify the excision axiom for singular homology. The tech-
niques involved in the proof will be useful later in other situations.

One of the facts we proved about simplicial complexes was that we could
chop up a finite complex barycentrically into simplices that were as small as
desired. We need a similar result for singular chains. To make this precise, we
shall use the following definition:

Definition 4.4.1 Suppose one is given a space X and a collection A of subsets

if its image set lies in an element of A.

In this section, we assume familiarity with Section 3.7, Categories and Func-
tors. The results of this section will be used when we prove the Eilenberg–
Zilber theorem in Section 7.9.

In the two preceding sections, we constructed certain natural chain homo-
topies DX. The method was to define DX first for a particular singular simplex
ip on a particular space ∆p. To do this, we needed the acyclicity of another
space, either ∆p × I [in Section 4.3] or of ∆p itself [in Section 4.4]. This
part of the construction involved an arbitrary choice; everything thereafter
was forced by naturality. The resemblance to earlier constructions involving
acyclic carriers was strong, but nevertheless, there were differences.

Now we formalize this method for later use. In this section, we state a
theorem, sufficiently strong for our purposes, that we shall call the acyclic
model theorem. Its formulation is sufficiently abstract to bother some readers.
To help you keep your feet on the ground, we will briefly review the meaning
of various terms from category theory that we will be using.

Note that if G is free relative to a collection M, then it is automatically
free relative to any larger collection. On the other hand, if G is acyclic relative
to M, then it is automatically acyclic relative to any smaller collection. Thus,
if we wish G to be both free and acyclic relative to M, then we must choose
M to be just the right size, neither too large nor too small.

Theorem 4.5.5 (Acyclic model theorem) Let G and G′ be functors from
the category C to the category A of augmented chain complexes and chain
maps of augmented chain complexes. Let M be a collection of objects of C.

If G is free relative to M and G′ is acyclic relative to M, then the following
hold:
(a) There is a natural transformation T of G to G′.
(b) Given two natural transformations S and T of G to G′, then
there is a natural chain homotopy D between S and T.

The method of acyclic models was first formalized by Eilenberg and

Definition 4.8.5 A nonempty Hausdorff space X is called an m-manifold if
each point of X has a neighborhood homeomorphic with an open subset of
euclidean space Rm. It is called an m-manifold with boundary if each point of
X has a neighborhood homeomorphic with an open subset of the euclidean
half-space Hm.

Note that an m-manifold is automatically an m-manifold with boundary.
For if x has a neighborhood homeomorphic with an open set in Rm, it has a
neighborhood U homeomorphic with an open ball in Rm. Then U is homeo-
morphic with the open unit ball in Rm centered at (0, 0, . . . , 0, 1), which is an
open set of Hm.

One often includes in the definition of a manifold the requirement that X
have a countable basis, or at least that X be metrizable. We shall not make
either assumption.

Manifolds and manifolds with boundary are among the most familiar and
important geometric objects. They are the main objects of study in differential
geometry and differential topology.

If X is a manifold with boundary and if h : U →V is a homeomorphism
of an open set U in X onto an open set V in Hm, then h is called a coordi-
nate patch on X. A point x of X may be mapped by h either into the upper
half space Rm−1 × R+ of Hm or onto the “edge” Rm−1 × 0. The local ho-
mology groups distinguish between these two possibilities. For it follows from
Example 4.8.4 that if x is mapped into the open upper half space of Hm,
then Hm(X, X \ x) is infinite cyclic, while if x is mapped into Bd Hm, then
Hm(X, X \ x) vanishes. This fact leads to the following definition:

Definition 4.8.6 Let X be an m-manifold with boundary. If the point x of
X maps to a point of Bd Hm under one coordinate patch about x, it maps
to a point of Bd Hm under every coordinate patch. Such a point is called a
boundary point of X. The set of all such points is called the boundary of X,
and is denoted Bd X. The space X \ Bd X is called the interior of X and is
denoted Int X.

Note that there is nothing in the definition requiring that X have any
boundary points. If it does not then Bd X is empty and X is an m-manifold.
While Bd X may be empty, the set Int X cannot be. For if h : U →V is
a coordinate patch about a point x of X, then V is open in Hm and hence
contains at least one point of the open upper half space. The corresponding
point y of X lies in Int X by definition.

We remark that the space Hm is itself an m-manifold with boundary, and
its boundary is precisely the set Rm−1 × 0, which we have already denoted by
Bd Hm. Similarly, Rm is itself an m-manifold.

Definition 4.8.7 Let X be an m-manifold with boundary. It follows from
Example 4.8.4 that m is uniquely determined by X, for it is the unique integer
such that the group Hm(X, X \ x) is non-trivial for at least one x in X. The
number m is called [of course] the dimension of the manifold with boundary
X.

EXAMPLE 4.8.9 Let σ be an n-simplex. Then σ is an n-manifold with

There is a certain overlapping of terminology here, which we should clarify.
In general topology, if A is a subset of a space X, then the interior of A,
denoted Int A, is the union of all open sets of X contained in A. The boundary
of A, denoted Bd A, is the set A∩X \ A. In the special case where A is an open
set of X, it turns out that Bd A = A\A. We have used this terminology from
general topology earlier in this book. For instance, the notion Bd U appeared
in Lemma 1.2.7, and the notion Int A was used in formulating the excision
axiom.

The concepts of boundary and interior for a manifold with boundary are
entirely different. It is unfortunate that the same terminology is commonly
used in two different ways. Some authors use ∂X to denote the boundary of
a manifold with boundary. But that leads to difficulty when one wishes to
distinguish the boundary of the space σ from the simplicial chain ∂σ. As is
usual in mathematics, we will simply endure some ambiguity, relying on the
context to make the meaning clear.

It happens that for the subset Bn of the topological space Rn, its boundary
in the sense of general topology is the same as its boundary in the sense of
manifolds with boundary. The same remark applies to the subspace Hn of Rn.
But it is safest to think of these cases being the exception rather than the
rule.

of the apparent holes in one of the partial tori, unlike with an ordinary sphere,
that loop cannot be contracted to a point without at some time intersecting
the horned sphere.

Theorem 4.9.7 (Invariance of domain) Let U be an open set in Rn and
let f : U →Rn be continuous and one-to-one. Then f(U) is open in Rn and
f : U →f(U) is a homeomorphism.
Proof: Without loss of generality, we can replace Rn by Sn.

Step 1. Given a point y of f(U), we show that f(U) contains a neighborhood
of y. This will prove that f(U) is open in Sn.

Let x be the point of U such that f(x) = y. Choose an open ball B(x, ϵ)
centered at x with radius ϵ > 0 chosen small enough that the closure of the ball,
B(x, ϵ), lies in U. Set S(x, ϵ) = B(x, ϵ)\B(x, ϵ). See Figure 4.9.5. Now the set
f(S(x, ϵ)) is homeomorphic to Sn−1. By Theorem 4.9.5, f(S(x, ϵ)) separates
Sn into two components W1 and W2, each open in Sn. The set f(B(x, ϵ)) is
connected and disjoint from f(S(x, ϵ)). Therefore, it lies in either W1 or W2.
Renaming if necessary, we may assume it lies in W1. Now it must equal all of
W1, for otherwise the set
Sn \ [f(B(x, ϵ)) ∪f(S(x, ϵ))] = Sn \ f(B(x, ϵ))

would consist of all of W2 along with points of W1 as well, contradicting
Theorem 4.9.3 which tells us that the cell f(B(x, ϵ)) does not separate Sn.
Therefore, f(B(x, ϵ)) = W1. We conclude that f(U) contains the neighbor-
hood W1 of y, as desired.

Step 2. In view of Step 1, f carries any set open in U to a set that is open in
Sn and hence open in f(U). Thus f is a homeomorphism of U with f(U).

The Fundamental Group

In this section we will give a brief introduction to homotopy theory, and look
particularly at the fundamental group of a space. One of the motivations for
homotopy theory is identifying and classifying the “holes” in a topological
space. The annulus has a hole in its center, and so does the unit sphere. See
Figure 4.10.1. But one has a sense that these two holes are different in nature.
They are, perhaps, holes of different dimensions. Homotopy theory helps us
to sort out these ideas.

4.11
More on Quotient Spaces

We reviewed some aspects of the theory of quotient spaces in Section 2.8. We
now discuss the topic further. In particular, we consider separation axioms for
quotient spaces.

We have already noted that the separation axioms do not behave well
for quotient spaces. In general, it is difficult to ensure that a quotient space
satisfies any stronger separation axiom than the T1-axiom. Even the Hausdorff
axiom is often hard to verify. We give here three situations in which we can
be sure that the quotient space is Hausdorff, indeed, normal.

We have already defined what it means for the topology of a given space
X to be coherent with a collection of subspaces of X. We wish to deal with
the separation axioms in this context.

First, we extend the notion of coherent topology slightly. We suppose that
we have a collection of topological spaces {Xα} whose union X has no topol-
ogy. We seek to find conditions under which there exists a topology on X,
of which the Xα are subspaces, such that this topology is coherent with the
subspaces Xα.

Lemma 4.11.4 Let X be a set that is the union of the topological spaces
{Xα}.
(a) If there is a topological space XT having X as its underlying set,

and each Xα is a subspace of XT , then X has a topology, of which
the Xα are subspaces, that is coherent with the Xα. This topology
is in general finer than the topology of XT .
(b) If, for each pair α, β of indices, the set Xα∩Xβ is closed in both

Xα and Xβ, and inherits the same subspace topology from each of
them, then X has a topology coherent with the subspaces Xα. Each
Xα is a closed set in this topology.

Proof:
(a) By hypothesis, we are given the topological space XT with un-
derlying set X. Let us define a [possibly different] topological space XC whose
underlying set is X by declaring a set A to be closed in XC if and only if its
intersection with each Xα is a closed subset of Xα. The collection of such sets
contains arbitrary intersections and finite unions of its elements, so it does
define a topology on the set X.

If A is closed in XT , then because Xα is a subspace of XT , the set A ∩Xα
is closed in Xα for each α. It follows that A is closed in XC. Thus the topology
of XC is finer than that of XT .

We next show that each Xα is a subspace of XC. It then follows from its
definition that XC is coherent with the subspaces Xα. For this purpose, we
show that the collection of closed sets of Xα equals the collection of sets of the
form A ∩Xα, where A is closed in XC. By the definition of XC, if A is closed
in XC, then A ∩Xα is closed in Xα. Conversely, suppose that B is closed in
Xα. Because Xα is a subspace of XT , we have B = A ∩Xα for some set A
closed in XT . Because the topology of XC is finer than that of XT , the set A
is also closed in XC. Thus B = A ∩Xα for some A closed in XC, as desired.

(b) As in part (a), we define the topology XC on the set X by declaring A
to be closed in XC if and only if A ∩Xα is closed in Xα for each α.

We show that each Xα is a subspace of XC. It then follows from its defini-
tion that XC is coherent with the subspaces Xα. As before, we show that the
collection of closed sets of Xα equals the collection of sets of the form A∩Xα,
where A is closed in XC. First, if A is closed in XC, then A ∩Xα is closed
in Xα. Conversely, suppose B is closed in Xα. Let β be any index. Because
Xα ∩Xβ is a closed set in Xα, the set

is a closed set of Xα. Because Xα ∩Xβ is a subspace of Xα, it is also a closed

We have stated that one of the advantages of simplicial homology theory is
its effective computability. On the other hand, the amount of labor involved
in a straightforward calculation in all but the simplest cases is too large to
carry out by hand. Even when we calculated the homology of such simple
spaces as the torus and the Klein bottle, in Section 1.7, we did not proceed

268
Elements of Algebraic Topology

straightforwardly. Instead, we used geometric arguments—of a rather ad hoc
nature—to reduce the computations to simpler ones.

We now refine these ad hoc techniques into a systematic method for com-
puting homology groups. This method will apply not only to simplicial homol-
ogy, but to singular homology as well. We introduce in this section a notion of
complex more general than that of the simplicial complex. It was invented by
J. H. C. Whitehead and introduced in [Whi49]. It is called a “CW complex.”
In the next section, we show how to assign to each CW complex a certain chain
complex, called its “cellular chain complex,” which can be used to compute
the homology of the underlying space. This chain complex is much simpler
and easier to deal with than the singular or simplicial chain complexes. In a
final section, we apply these methods to compute, among other things, the
homology of real and complex projective spaces.

Definition 4.12.1 Recall that a space is called a cell of dimension m if it
is homeomorphic with Bm. It is called an open cell of dimension m if it is
homeomorphic with Int Bn. In each case the integer m is uniquely determined
by the space in question.

Definition 4.12.2 A CW complex is a space X and a collection of disjoint
open cells eα whose union is X such that:
(2) For each open m-cell of the collection, there exists a continuous

map fα : Bm →X that maps Int Bm homeomorphically onto eα and
carries Bd Bm into a finite union of open cells, each of dimension
less than m.
(3) A set A is closed in X if A ∩eα is closed in eα for each α.

The finiteness part of condition (2) was called “closure-finiteness” by J.
H. C. Whitehead. Condition (3) expresses the fact that X has what he called
the “weak topology” relative to the collection {eα}. These terms are the origin
of the letters “C” and “W” in the phrase “CW complex.”

We typically denote eα \ eα by ˙eα. We remark that conditions (1) and (2)
imply that f carries Bm onto eα and Bd Bm onto ˙eα. To see these facts, note
that because fα is continuous, it carries Bm, which is the closure of Int Bm,
into the closure of fα(Int Bm), which is eα. Because fα(Bm) is compact, it is
closed [since X is Hausdorff]. Because it contains eα it must contain eα. Thus
we have fα(Bm) = eα. Finally, because fα(Bd Bm) is disjoint from eα it must
equal ˙eα.

We remark also that the converse of (3) holds trivially: If A is closed in
X, then A ∩eα is closed in eα for each α.

The map fα is called the “characteristic map” for the open cell eα. Note
that the maps fα are not uniquely specified in the definition of a CW complex.
Only the space X and the collection {eα} are specified. We customarily abuse

Singular Homology Theory
269

notation and use the symbol X to refer to both the CW complex and to the
underlying space.

A finite CW complex X is a CW complex for which the collection of open
cells is finite. If X has only finitely many open cells, then the finiteness part
of (2) is automatic, and condition (3) is implied by the other conditions: If
the set A ∩eα is closed in eα, then it is closed in X; thus since A is a finite
union of such sets, A is also closed in X.

A finite CW complex is of course compact. Conversely, any compact subset
A of a CW complex X can intersect only finitely many open cells of X. We
leave the proof to the exercises. One needs the finiteness part of condition (2)
in the proof.

The following lemma is an immediate consequence of our general results
about coherent topologies [see Section 2.8].

Lemma 4.12.3 Let X be a CW complex with the open cells eα. A function
f : X →Y is continuous if and only if f|eα is continuous for each α. A
function F : X × I →Y is continuous if and only if F|(eα × I) is continuous
for each α.

Similarly, one can express the Klein bottle as a CW complex having the

can be expressed as a CW complex having one open cell in dimension 2, one

Y ∩eβ ⊂˙eβ, so Y ∩eβ lies in the union of finitely many open cells of Y , say
e1, e2, . . . , ek. Then

We now see how strong the analogy is between the homology of simpli-

For each open p-cell eα of the CW complex X, the group Hp(eα, ˙eα) is
infinite cyclic. The two generators of this group will be called the two orien-
tations of eα. An oriented p-cell of X is an open p-cell eα together with an
orientation of eα.

The cellular chain group Dp(X) = Hp(Xp, Xp−1) is a free abelian group.
One obtains a basis for it by orienting each open p-cell eα of X and passing
to the corresponding element of Hp(Xp, Xp−1). [That is, by taking the image

In the special case where X is a triangulable CW complex triangulated by a
complex K, and Hp denotes simplicial homology, we interpret these comments

by eα whose boundaries are carried by ˙eα. This group is infinite cyclic, and
either generator of this group is called a fundamental cycle for (eα, ˙eα).

The cellular chain group Dp(X) equals the group of all simplicial p-chains
of X carried by Xp whose boundaries are carried by Xp−1. Any such p-chain
can be written uniquely as a finite linear combination of fundamental cycles
for those pairs (eα, ˙eα) for which dim eα = p.

We now apply the theory of CW complexes to compute the homology of

Remark 4.14.16 The converse of Theorem 4.14.15 is true, but the proof is
very difficult.

In a 1935 paper [see [Rei35]], Kurt Reidemeister defined a number associ-
ated with a simplicial complex called its torsion. The torsion is a combinatorial
invariant, which means that two complexes that have isomorphic subdivisions
necessarily have the same torsion. By computing the torsion for lens spaces,
Reidemeister showed that if the simplicial complexes L(n, k) and L(n, ℓ) have
isomorphic subdivisions, then either k ≡±ℓ(mod n) or kℓ≡±1 (mod n).

To complete the proof of the converse, we need to appeal to work of E. E.
Moise from the 1950s. Moise wrote a series of papers concerning “affine struc-

With each topological space X we have associated a sequence of abelian groups
called its homology groups. Now we associate with X another sequence of
abelian groups, called its cohomology groups. These groups were not defined
until long after the homology groups. The reason is not hard to understand,
for they are geometrically much less natural than the homology groups. Their
origins lie in algebra rather than geometry. In a certain algebraic sense [to
be made precise later], they are “dual” to the homology groups. In the past,
topologists have used such terms as “pseudo-cycle” for representatives of these
group elements, implying a certain skepticism as to their legitimacy as objects
of study. Eventually, it became clear that these groups are both important in
theory and useful in practice. The cohomology groups are more subtle than
the homology groups, and much more profound and powerful. We shall learn
about them in this chapter.

The duality theorems for manifolds, the connections between topology and
differential geometry [de Rham’s theorem] and between topology and analysis
[cohomology with sheaf coefficients]—all these results are formulated in terms
of cohomology. Even such purely topological problems as classifying spaces
up to homeomorphism, or maps up to homotopy, are problems about which
cohomology has a good deal to say. We will return to some of these problems
later.

Throughout this chapter we assume familiarity with the language of cate-
gories and functors [Section 3.7].

Associated with any pair of abelian groups A and G is a third abelian group,
the group Hom (A, G) of all homomorphisms of A into G. This group will be
involved in an essential way in the definition of the cohomology groups. In
this section we study some of its properties.

manifold if the following hold:
(1) The closure of |K| \ |K0| equals a union of n-simplices.

is a sequence of n-simplices of K, not in K0,
such that σi ∩σi+1 is an (n −1)-simplex not in K0, for each i.
If K0 = ∅, then we call K a pseudo n-manifold.

5.6
The Cohomology of Free Chain Complexes

Until now, we have computed the cohomology groups only for a few simple
spaces. We wish to compute them more generally. We shall prove that, for a
CW complex X, the cellular chain complex D(X), which we know can be used
to compute the homology of X, can be used to compute the cohomology as
well. This we shall prove in Section 5.8. The proof depends on two theorems
about free chain complexes that we prove in this section.

The first theorem states that, for free chain complexes C and D, any ho-
momorphism Hp(C) →Hp(D) of homology groups is induced by a chain map
ϕ. The second theorem states that if a chain map ϕ : C →D of free chain com-
plexes induces an isomorphism in homology, then it induces an isomorphism
in cohomology as well. An independent proof of the second theorem will be
given in Chapter 7, so you can simply assume this theorem for the time being
if you wish.

Remark 5.6.8 Let us explain the geometric motivation underlying the defi-
nition of the chain complex D′.

In homotopy theory, there is a standard construction for, roughly speaking,
replacing an arbitrary continuous map h : X →Y by an imbedding of X in
a space that is homotopy equivalent to Y . More precisely, there is a space Y ′
and imbeddings i and j such that the diagram

commutes up to homotopy, and such that j is a homotopy equivalence. It
follows at once that h is a homotopy equivalence if and only if i is. In this
way problems concerning the map h are reduced to problems concerning the
imbedding i.

This construction is called the mapping cylinder construction. We describe
it here, and explain how the chain complex D′ is an algebraic analogue.

Given h : X →Y , let us form a quotient space from the disjoint union of
X × I and Y by identifying each point (x, 0) of X × 0 with the point h(x) of
Y . The resulting adjunction space Y ′ is called the mapping cylinder of h. We
picture it as looking something like a top hat. See Figure 5.6.1

pushes down the top hat onto j(Y ). Just as clearly, the map i : X →Y ′ is
homotopic to the map j ◦h: again, one simply pushes i(X) down.

The results of Section 5.6 tell us that, if the homology groups fail to distinguish
between two spaces, then the cohomology groups will fail as well. One might
be tempted to ask, “Why bother with cohomology? What possible use can it
be?”

There are several answers to this question. One answer is that cohomology
appears naturally when one studies the problem of classifying, up to homo-
topy, maps of one space into another. Another answer is that cohomology is
involved when one integrates differential forms on manifolds. Yet another an-
swer is the one given in this section. We show that the cohomology groups
have an additional algebraic structure—that of a ring—and that this ring will
distinguish between spaces when the groups themselves will not.

We shall define the ring structure of cohomology by giving a specific
cochain formula for the multiplication operation. Historically, this is how the
ring structure was first obtained. The formula was discovered about 1936 by

350
Elements of Algebraic Topology

Alexander, ˇCech, and Whitney. At the time, it seemed very mysterious. Its
geometric meaning was not at all clear. Furthermore, it was very puzzling why
there was a multiplication operation in cohomology, but not in homology.

In the case of a compact orientable manifold, it had been known for some
time that its homology had a ring structure. The multiplication in this ring
was called the intersection product, and it has a clear geometric meaning. But
all attempts to generalize this multiplication to more general spaces failed. It
was not until 1942, when Lefschetz gave a new definition of the multiplication
operation in cohomology, that it became clear why, for general spaces, there
exists a cohomology ring, but not a homology ring. It also became clear, about
the same time, what the relationship was between the homology and coho-
mology rings when both were defined: The Poincar´e duality theorem showed
that the two rings were isomorphic. We shall return to these matters later in
Sections 7.11 and 8.9.
Review of Rings, Modules, and Fields

We begin by reviewing some basic facts from algebra concerning rings and
modules.

A ring R is an abelian group, written additively, with a multiplication
operation, denoted · , satisfying two axioms:
(1) Associativity α · (β · γ) = (α · β) · γ.

(2) Distributivity
α · (β + γ) = α · β + α · γ,
(α + β) · γ = α · γ + β · γ.

[Absent parentheses, multiplications are performed before addi-
tions.]

If α · β = β · α for all α, β ∈R, then R is said to be commutative. If there is
an element 1 in R such that α · 1 = 1 · α = α for all α ∈R, then 1 is called a
unity element in R. If R has a unity element, then this element is easily seen
to be unique. Furthermore, one has (−1) · α = −α and 0 · α = 0 for all α ∈R.

If R is a commutative ring with unity, and if R satisfies the additional
condition that for every α̸ = 0, there is a β such that α · β = 1, then R is
called a field.

Now suppose A is an additive group and R is a commutative ring with
unity. We say that A has the structure of a module over R, or A is an R-module,
if there is a binary operation R × A →A [written as scalar multiplication]
such that for α, β ∈R and a, b ∈A we have
(1) α(a + b) = αa + αb.
(2) (α + β)a = αa + βa.

If A and B are R-modules, then a module homomorphism is a homomorphism
ϕ : A →B such that ϕ(αa) = αϕ(a) holds, for α ∈R and a ∈A. The kernel
and cokernel of such a homomorphism have natural R-module structures. In
the special case where R is a field F, we call A a vector space over F, and we
call the homomorphism ϕ a linear transformation.

We shall not have much occasion to deal with modules in this book. Our
primary concern will be with rings and vector spaces.

Cohomology Rings of Surfaces

There is no general method for computing the singular cohomology ring of X,
even if X is a CW complex. The reason is not hard to find: It turns out that
the cellular complex of X does not determine the cohomology ring of X. That
is, two CW complexes can have isomorphic cellular chain complexes without
having isomorphic cohomology rings!

this section, we define a simplicial cup product formula that corresponds to
the previous formula for singular cochains under the standard isomorphism of
simplicial theory with singular theory. Then we use this formula to compute
a number of examples.

Homology with Coefficients

After having studied cohomology with arbitrary coefficients, we now return to
a subject that was briefly introduced for the simplicial theory in Chapter 1—
homology with arbitrary coefficients.

To start with, we introduce an algebraic functor called the tensor prod-
uct and study its properties. This functor plays a role in homology theory
that is similar to that played by the Hom functor for cohomology. After that
introduction, we study homology with arbitrary coefficients.

If A and B are abelian groups, then of course their Cartesian product A×B is
an abelian group, and one often considers homomorphisms of the group A×B
into a third abelian group C. Sometimes it is important to consider functions
from A × B to C that are bilinear, that is, functions that are homomorphisms
when considered as function of each variable separately. In this section, we
define an abelian group called the tensor product of A and B, denoted A ⊗B,
that has the property that bilinear functions from A × B to C can naturally
be considered as homomorphisms from A ⊗B to C, and conversely. Thus the
study of bilinear functions is reduced to the familiar study of homomorphisms.

of A ⊗B. Rather, it tells us that a ⊗b is a typical generator of A ⊗B.

We have already seen, in Chapter 5, that two spaces with isomorphic homol-
ogy groups have isomorphic cohomology groups as well. This fact leads one to
suspect that the cohomology groups of a space are in some way determined by
the homology groups. In this chapter this suspicion is confirmed. We show pre-
cisely how the cohomology groups with arbitrary coefficients are determined by
the homology groups with integer coefficients. The theorem involved is called
the Universal Coefficient Theorem for Cohomology. Its statement involves not
only the Hom functor introduced in Section 5.2, but also a new functor called
“Ext” that we shall introduce in the next section.

Similarly, we know that if two spaces have isomorphic integral homology
groups, then the same is true for homology with arbitrary coefficients. Just
as with the cohomology groups, it turns out that the homology groups with
arbitrary coefficients are determined by the homology groups with integer
coefficients. The theorem involved is called the Universal Coefficient Theorem
for Homology. It involves not only the tensor product functor introduced in
Section 6.2, but also a new functor called the “torsion product” that we shall
introduce in Section 7.4.

The functors mentioned above form part of a general subject called homo-
logical algebra. Although its origins are topological in nature, it has come to
have an independent existence nowadays within the field of algebra, having
applications to many problems that are purely algebraic. Our interest in it is
confined to its connections with topology.

These functors also play a role when one comes to study the homology of a
product space X × Y . It turns out that the homology of X × Y is determined
by the homology of X and of Y . The relationship is expressed in the form of
an exact sequence called the K¨unneth sequence. It involves both the tensor
and torsion functors.

There is a similar sequence for cohomology that holds if the homology
is finitely generated. It has applications to cup products in general, and to
computing the cohomology ring of X × Y in particular.

We have stated two universal coefficient theorems that express the homology
and cohomology groups with arbitrary coefficients in terms of homology with
integer coefficients. One might ask whether for this purpose cohomology and
homology are symmetric in some sense—that is, whether these same groups
can be expressed in terms of cohomology with integer coefficients. In fact,

generality, but apply only if the homology groups Hi(C) are finitely generated.

cochain complex {Hom (Ci, Z), δ} so as to make it into a chain complex, and
then applying the universal coefficient theorems we have already considered.

free, so some restrictive hypotheses are needed.

7.10
∗The K¨unneth Theorem for Cohomolgy

of a product space, which we shall study in the next section.

As we have mentioned before, manifolds are among the most familiar and im-
portant geometric objects in mathematics. It took quite some time for math-
ematicians to produce a rigorous definition of the manifold concept. It was
Hermann Weyl, in his book on Riemann surfaces,1 who finally nailed down
the idea.

Any theorems that we can prove about manifolds are likely to be useful,
not only in topology, but also in differential geometry and other branches of
mathematics. The duality theorems are examples of such theorems.

We already know one relationship that holds between the homology and
cohomology groups of an arbitrary topological space; it is expressed by the
universal coefficient theorem for cohomology. For manifolds, there is a sec-
ond such relationship. It is expressed in the famous Poincar´e duality theorem.
If we think of the universal coefficient theorem as expressing a sort of alge-
braic duality between cohomology and homology, then Poincar´e duality can
be thought of as fundamentally geometric in nature. This duality does not
hold for an arbitrary space, but depends specifically on properties possessed
by manifolds.

There is a certain amount of interplay between these geometric and alge-
braic types of duality. This interplay has some interesting applications—we
shall apply it to the problem of computing the cohomology ring of a manifold.

There are further duality theorems. They bear the names of Lefschetz,
Alexander, and Pontryagin. We shall study them in due course. All are con-
cerned with algebraic-topological properties of manifolds.

Throughout this discussion, we assume familiarity with local homology
groups [Section 4.8].

Definition 8.2.8 Let s be a simplex of the complex K. The star of s in K,

v0, v1, . . . , vn is positive. That is,

8.3
Homology Manifolds

In this section we shall define homology manifolds and obtain some of their
local properties. The class of homology manifolds includes all topological man-
ifolds, so it is a broad and important collection of spaces. The triangulable
homology manifolds will be the basic objects involved in the various duality
theorems.

For convenience, we shall deal with the case of relative homology manifolds
in the present section, even though we shall not actually prove the duality
theorems in the relative case until Section 8.10.

We begin now by recording a convention. We shall be dealing with tri-
angulable spaces. If X is such a space with a specific triangulation, then we
shall frequently abuse notation and make no notational distinction between
the space and the complex triangulating it. For instance, we may refer to a
point of [the space] X or to a simplex of [the complex] X. The meaning in
each instance will be made clear from context.

Definition 8.3.1 A topological pair (X, A) is called a relative homology n-
manifold if for each point x of X not in A, the local homology group Hi(X, X\
x) vanishes if i̸ = n and is infinite cyclic if i = n. In the case where A is empty,
we refer to X simply as a homology n-manifold.

The Dual Block Complex

For simplicity we are going to restrict ourselves in the next few sections to the
case of a homology n-manifold X. The techniques that we use will reappear
later when we consider the case of a relative homology manifold.

There is associated with the triangulated homology manifold X a certain
partition of X into subsets that are [almost] open cells such that X becomes
[almost] a regular cell complex. The subsets are not actual topological cells
but only homological cells. Since we cannot call them “cells,” we shall instead
call them “blocks.” And we shall call the collection of these blocks the dual
block decomposition of X. Just as there was with cell complexes, there is a
chain complex associated to this block complex that can be used to compute
the homology and cohomology of X. We will call it the “dual chain complex.”
It will be a crucial tool in proving our duality theorems.

8.5
Poincar´e Duality

The Poincar´e duality theorem is one of the most profound results in all of
topology. In its original form, it stated that for a compact, orientable, trian-
gulated n-manifold X, the betti numbers in dimensions k and n−k were equal
and the torsion numbers in dimensions k and n −k −1 were equal. Nowa-
days, it is stated in a different but equivalent formulation. Today we state
that the homology and cohomology groups of X in dimensions k and n −k
are isomorphic.

There are also versions of Poincar´e duality that hold when X is not ori-
entable, or when X is not compact. We shall discuss these too.

We shall give two proofs of Poincar´e duality. The first of these, which we
give in the present section, is rather straightforward and intuitive. The second,
which we will consider in Section 8.7, will provide valuable information on how
the duality isomorphism behaves with respect to continuous maps. It also gives
information about cup products on manifolds.

We say that X is orientable if it is possible to orient all the n-simplices σi
of X so that their sum γ =  σi is a cycle. Such a cycle γ will be called an
orientation cycle for X.

Given the ring structure in cohomology, defined by the cup product, the

The intersection product α · β of two homology classes was defined, roughly

Defining the homology intersection ring in this way, and deriving its proper-

it was not preserved by continuous maps, even between manifolds of the same

Nowadays we view the matter differently. We consider the cohomology
ring as the natural object and view the existence of the homology intersection
ring for manifolds as a happy accident resulting from the Poincar´e duality
isomorphism.

8.13
ˇCech Cohomology

Until now we have studied two homology and cohomology theories—namely,
the simplicial theory and the singular theory. There are a number of oth-
ers, most notably the ˇCech theory. This theory turns out to be particularly
satisfactory in the case of cohomology. This is what we discuss now.

We shall construct the ˇCech cohomology groups of a topological space and
show that they agree with the simplicial groups when both are defined. We also
construct a topological space for which the ˇCech and singular theories disagree.
We shall use ˇCech cohomology in the next section to prove a generalized
version of Alexander duality.
We begin with the concept of a directed set.
